item.title: DDR5 Costs Five Times More. My 2013 Workstation Runs a 125B Model Anyway.
item.guid: title:ddr5 costs five times more my 2013 workstation runs a 125b model anyway
item.description: 38 to 48 tokens per second from a Xeon without AVX2 and two 2017 GPUs, and what three home PCs taught me about where local LLM speed really comes from. The X79 up close: two used Titan Xp cards from 2017, the Xeon’s cooler at the top right and, on the left, a four-slot M. 2 adapter of which this 2011 board can use only the first slot. “Many people show off by spending thousands of euros on technology built by someone else, just to keep up with fashion. I dig into technology to squeeze everything out of it, recycling included. ” That is how I described my approach this week, and I think it is a fairly cyberpunk way to do AI at home.

item.title: Setting the Scene (Public v1; October 25)
item.guid: title:setting the scene public v1 october 25
item.description: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a refresher on recent events, but also as a hook to draw students into engaging with some of ideas we think about and debate in AI safety early. I expect the topics I cover in my “Setting the Scene” post to change frequently, so this is less polished than some of my other content. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Any feedback on how to improve these posts would be greatly appreciated. Cyber Security I think it’s worth reflecting that it is a particularly pertinent time to be doing a course on AI safety.

item.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
item.guid: title:kimi k3 open frontier intelligence
item.description: Today, we are introducing Kimi K3 — our most capable model. Kimi K3 is a 2. 8T-parameter model built on our Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, with native vision capabilities and a 1-million-token context window. It is the world's first open 3T-class model, designed for frontier intelligence across long-horizon coding, knowledge work, and reasoning. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5. 6 Sol, Kimi K3 demonstrated frontier-level performance across our evaluation suite, consistently outperforming other tested models.

item.title: Week in AI Careers: Who Gets the AI Jobs, and Who Doesn’t
item.guid: title:week in ai careers who gets the ai jobs and who doesn t
item.description: Two data releases last week put numbers on who the AI labor market is lifting and who it is passing over. The Pew Research Center found that men have captured almost all of the job growth in AI-exposed occupations since generative AI arrived, while women’s employment in those roles has stayed flat. Goldman Sachs economist Joseph Briggs estimated that up to 9 percent of workers could be displaced during the AI transition, though he expects the cuts to cluster in a recession rather than arrive at a steady pace. Governments moved too: New York committed 10 million dollars to train 40,000 residents for AI work at a new Queens institute, and Italy’s workplace AI rules took effect requiring a human to make the final call on hiring and firing. Quick Hits cover a federal AI-workforce grant, a manufacturing training partnership, and new research on AI hiring tools, followed by the two ODSC events. Surveys and research Pew finds men capturing nearly all job growth in AI-exposed work What happened: The Pew Research Center reported on October 22 that employment growth in AI-exposed occupations has gone almost entirely to men since generative AI became widely available.

item.title: Building a Synthetic Data Pipeline
item.guid: title:building a synthetic data pipeline
item.description: Why Teams Start Building a Synthetic Data Pipeline Most teams arrive at building a synthetic data pipeline the same way: a dataset is collected, a model is trained, the metrics look acceptable, and then the model fails in production on inputs nobody thought to collect. The usual response is to collect more data, and that works until it does not. Collection takes weeks, annotation takes longer, and the scenarios that break a model appear least often in the real world. Three pressures make the case: Privacy and restricted data. Much real data cannot leave the environment it came from, and principles such as GDPR data minimization limit how widely it can be copied. Public datasets rarely match production conditions.

item.title: Why I Started Talking to My Computer Instead of Typing at It
item.guid: title:why i started talking to my computer instead of typing at it
item.description: Reading Is a 5,000-Year-Old Hack. Speaking Is a 200,000-Year-Old Operating System. Before any human could read a single word, every human could tell a story, and anyone within earshot could receive it. That asymmetry is close to 200,000 years old on one side and roughly 5,000 years old on the other. Spoken language, as far as the fossil and genetic evidence can tell us, is old enough to be load-bearing in our neurology. Writing is a tool we bolted on afterward: a clever hack that happens to work, not a native capacity we were born wired for.

item.title: Introducing PerceptionBench
item.guid: title:introducing perceptionbench
item.description: Evaluating Atomic Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models Authors Kimi Team We are releasing PerceptionBench , a benchmark that isolates visual perception and evaluates it as a set of atomic capabilities— discovered from how today's models fail, not defined in advance. From frontier-model failures across 42 benchmarks, we derive 10 atomic perceptual capabilities and construct 3,000 verified questions, each isolating a single capability and answerable by looking, with no reasoning or external knowledge required.

item.title: The Interpretability team studies how large language models work internally as a foundation for AI safety. They seek to understand what happens inside neural networks so that we can better trust the models we build.
item.guid: title:the interpretability team studies how large language models work internally as a foundation for ai safety they seek to understand what happens inside neural networks so that we can better trust the models we build
item.description: It’s hard to reason about the safety of neural networks without understanding what happens inside them. Our goal is to be able to explain large language models’ behavior, and to use that understanding to identify problems that are hard to see from the outside, such as situations where a model’s stated reasoning differs from what it’s actually doing. Our early work focused on mapping the internal mechanisms of AI models. Today, we increasingly apply our methods to real models to understand how they think and why they behave the way they do. We’ve developed techniques that allow us to understand models’ inner workings in plain language, making it easier to detect unsafe behavior or dishonest reasoning and safeguard against it. item.title: Open Source Code Review Tools for GitHub and Self-Hosted Teams
item.guid: title:open source code review tools for github and self hosted teams
item.description: Open source code review tools fall into two groups, and search results often mix them. Open source code review tools for GitHub run inside pull requests you already have: a GitHub Action or a CLI posts on the pull request, and the repository stays on GitHub. Self-hosted Git forges and review servers are the other group: they are where the repository, or the review request, lives. MergeJudge (mergejudge. si) is an AI pull request reviewer with an open-source engine for GitHub. The engine, the Action and the runner CLI are MIT-licensed in gauravsharmaGG/mergejudge-runner .

item.title: Exploring Open-Source Large Language Models for InkMind: Choosing a Better Poetry Continuation Model
item.guid: title:exploring open source large language models for inkmind choosing a better poetry continuation model
item.description: Exploring Open-Source Large Language Models for InkMind: Choosing a Better Poetry Continuation Model Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have become important tools in natural language processing (NLP). They can generate text, summarize information, answer questions, and assist with creative writing. Most modern text-generating LLMs use the Transformer architecture and learn patterns in language from large collections of text. Our project, InkMind , focuses on poetry generation through text continuation. Unlike an instruction-based chatbot, InkMind receives an opening phrase or part of a poem and generates the following words. For example, given the input “Beneath the moon, I walk alone,” the model should continue the text in a coherent and creative way.

item.title: Kimi Introduces Agent Swarm: Let 100 AI Agents Work for You
item.guid: title:kimi introduces agent swarm let 100 ai agents work for you
item.description: In 2025, if you walked into any AI conference, you may hear the same gospel: faster inference, longer context windows, cheaper inference costs. It's as if we've spent years perfecting the hammer, making it lighter, stronger, more precisely balanced, while never questioning the fact that the carpenter still has only two hands and twenty-four hours in a day. Now, Kimi introduces Agent Swarm. It is not a better hammer. It is a reconstruction of the entire workshop.

item.title: Web Pages Can Command AI Coding Agents: Over 90% Success Through the Downloads Folder
item.guid: title:web pages can command ai coding agents over 90 success through the downloads folder
item.description: Browsers save files to Downloads without user interaction, while AI agents automatically follow instruction files. These two behaviors, neither a bug on its own, combine to let a single text file trigger malware execution, as demonstrated with Codex and Claude Code. Key points What happened: An AGENTS. md file in the Downloads folder was instructing an AI coding agent to install the function-color malware Why it works: A structural gap that no one can patch lies at the intersection of browsers saving files to Downloads without user interaction and agents automatically following instruction files How to prevent it: Do not launch agents in Downloads; check unfamiliar instruction files and configuration changes. Instructions to disable approval prompts are themselves a sign of an attack The day Markdown became an executable Forever Security, which monitors the security of AI coding agents, detected a coding agent attempting to install the malicious npm package function-color on a customer's computer and blocked it before execution . function-color is known malware belonging to the MALFEX campaign reported by Checkmarx on October 5, 2026.
